def tuiles(elements):
    """Key-figure tiles, in simple responsive HTML."""
    cases = "".join(f'<div style="flex:1 1 150px;border:1px solid #e1e0d9;border-radius:6px;padding:.7em .9em;background:#fcfcfb">'

This page presents the main series used to explain the price of cocoa. The project has 28 in total, grouped into 8 families. All are aligned on cocoa trading days, from 3 January 2005 to 3 November 2026, i.e. 5,489 sessions.

Basic rule: a data point is used only after its publication. For example, October rainfall is only published at the end of November: the model only sees it from that date. Without this rule, the model would “cheat” by using information that nobody knew yet.

What this page is for. The aim of the project is to anticipate the future price of cocoa. This page helps understand each data source: what it measures, when it becomes available, through which mechanism it could affect the price, and what the tests actually showed. Details of the 328 columns are in the dictionary of variables.

A raw column is not always a model variable. The climate family has 181 columns, but many are used for robustness tests (NASA rainfall, GEFS forecasts) or concern countries that were not retained. The models receive about 140 transformed variables, computed from these columns (Families page).

The 8 data families

For each family: what it measures, through which channel it could affect the price, with what lag, and what the tests showed. Channels and lags are economic hypotheses, not demonstrated causal links.

  • Channels: direct supply and demand, production costs (indirect), investor expectations (financial), shocks and regime changes.
  • Lags: immediate (days), delayed (months), structural (years).

Assumed mechanism. Abnormal rainfall or heat in growing areas could reduce the coming harvest; the market would react as soon as it anticipates it.

Item Content
Channel Direct supply; climate shocks (El Niño)
Assumed lag of effect Delayed: a season’s weather affects the harvest of the following months
Dataset columns 131 raw columns (all countries), giving 42 transformed variables in the model; details in the dictionary
Sources CHIRPS v2.0, ERA5, NASA POWER, NOAA Climate Prediction Center
Native frequency daily, monthly
Publication lag applied 3 days (delay observed on the API in November 2026); 45 days after the end of the season (cautious assumption, to be confirmed); 6 days (delay observed on the API in November 2026); 7 days (observed API delay); The 25th of the following month (margin above the announced 3rd week)
Period available 01/2005 to 11/2026

What the tests showed.

  • A. Economic relevance: plausible mechanism (hypothesis above), not demonstrated.
  • B. Statistical information (association in the 2010-2026 sample, multiple-testing correction): 0 association retained out of 210 with the future return, 38 out of 168 with future volatility.
  • C. Out-of-sample predictive power: removing it clearly worsens the model for: no target. Removing it improves it for: direction 60, volatility 20. But no factor model beats the benchmark: the family brings no demonstrated gain over a model without factors.

    elif serie == "FEUX_CIV":

From data to forecasts

A data source can make strong economic sense without improving the price forecast. Three measures must be distinguished, and none proves causality:

Measure Question Where it is computed
Importance in the model (SHAP) What does the model rely on? Families page
Statistical association Does the variable move with the future price, in sample? Below
Marginal out-of-sample contribution (family removal) Does the model forecast worse without it? Families page
Show the code 
lignes = []
for fam in FAMILIES:
    a = asso[asso["famille"] == fam]
    rr = retrait[retrait["famille"] == fam]
    for cible, h in [("rendement", h) for h in (1, 5, 20, 60, 120)] + [("vol", h) for h in (5, 20, 60, 120)]:
        x = a[(a["cible"] == cible) & (a["horizon"] == h)]
        y = rr[(rr["cible"] == ("sens" if cible == "rendement" else "vol")) & (rr["horizon"] == h)]
        lignes.append({"famille": FAMILIES[fam], "cible": f"{'Dir.' if cible == 'rendement' else 'Vol.'} {h}",
                       "assoc": int(x["retenue_fdr_5pct"].sum()), "n": len(x),
                       "perte": float(y["perte"].iloc[0]) if len(y) else np.nan, "sig": bool(len(y) and (y["ic_bas"].iloc[0] > 0 or y["ic_haut"].iloc[0] < 0))})
t = pd.DataFrame(lignes)
ordre = [f"Dir. {h}" for h in (1, 5, 20, 60, 120)] + [f"Vol. {h}" for h in (5, 20, 60, 120)]
m = t.pivot(index="famille", columns="cible", values="assoc").reindex(columns=ordre)
txt = t.assign(v=t["assoc"].astype(str) + "/" + t["n"].astype(str)).pivot(index="famille", columns="cible", values="v").reindex(columns=ordre)
fig = go.Figure(go.Heatmap(z=m.to_numpy(), x=ordre, y=m.index, colorscale=[[0, "#f0efec"], [1, "#2a78d6"]], text=txt.to_numpy(),
                           texttemplate="%{text}", xgap=2, ygap=2, colorbar=dict(thickness=10, title="Variables"),
                           hovertemplate="%{y}<br>%{x}<br>Associations retained: %{text}<extra></extra>"))
fig.update_layout(title="Statistical information: variables associated with the future target (multiple-testing correction)", height=400,
                  xaxis=dict(side="top"), yaxis=dict(automargin=True, autorange="reversed"), margin=dict(t=110))
fig.show()

What this table shows.

  • Future return: 2 associations out of 710 trials (direction at 5 sessions: change in producers’ positions; direction at 120 sessions: nitrogen in Côte d’Ivoire). This is barely more than chance would produce, and it did not translate into better out-of-sample forecasts.
  • Future volatility: many variables are associated with it, especially past cocoa volatility, geopolitical risk and news. But part of these associations simply reflects the crisis period, when everything is turbulent at the same time. Out of sample, the HAR model, which only uses past volatility, remains the best.
  • Overall reading: the data contain information on the size of moves, already captured by the past price. They contain almost none on their direction. This is why no family beats the models without factors (Results and Exploratory leads pages).

The price of cocoa

What we look at. The cocoa futures contract listed in New York (ICE, Yahoo symbol CC=F), in dollars per tonne. A futures contract is a commitment to buy or sell cocoa at a future date. Its price reflects what the market expects about supply and demand.

Why it is interesting. For almost twenty years the price stayed between 2,000 and 4,000 $/t, then it passed 10,000 $/t in 2024. The project seeks to know whether factors such as weather, costs, investors or geopolitics made it possible to anticipate these moves.

A technical trap. CC=F chains contracts together: when a contract expires, Yahoo switches to the next one, and the price can jump without any real market move, by up to 30% in 2024. The models account for this through a control reading, which removes these jumps (Method page).

Quality of the CC=F series, the models’ target

How Yahoo builds CC=F. CC=F follows a single contract at a time, the front month, then switches to the next. Prices are not spliced (no back-adjustment): at each switch, the price gap between the two contracts shows up as a spurious return.

How the project detects the switches (scripts/03 and src/cacao/grille.py):

  1. Before expiry, Yahoo stays on the expiring contract while trading has already moved to the next one: volume collapses. A roll is detected when volume rises back above 1,000 contracts after 3 sessions below 100.
  2. The jump day is the day with the largest absolute return between that day and the next.
  3. Treatment: no corrected series is published. The models are also judged in the control reading: windows without a roll up to 20 sessions, jump-day return set to zero at 60 and 120 sessions.

Limit: this detection is done after the fact (it uses the next day’s volume and return). It is only used for evaluation, never as a variable.

No corrected series is therefore produced. The three active contracts (December 2026, March and May 2027) nonetheless make it possible to check the latest roll.

fig.show()
  • Until 15 September 2026, CC=F follows the September contract, absent from Yahoo, below the December contract. The gap closes as expiry approaches.
  • CC=F becomes identical to the December contract on 16 September 2026. Volume-based detection had dated this roll to 15 September: one day apart. It is the only roll that can be checked against individual contracts.
  • The gap between March 2027 and December 2026 ranges from −3.1% to +2.4% depending on the day: this is the order of magnitude of the spurious return at the next roll, in the current market.

The jump-free series drifts away from the actual price as rolls accumulate. It is therefore useful for measuring returns, not as a price level. Against the World Bank monthly price (ICCO), raw CC=F is in fact closer (correlation 0.993) than the jump-free version (0.935). This is why the project keeps raw CC=F as the reference and tests robustness in the control reading.

Do the artefacts degrade the forecasts?

Show the code

v = cq.pivot(index="horizon", columns="serie", values=["vol_moyenne", "rmse_persistance", "rmse_har"]).round(3)
v.columns = [f"{a} ({b})" for a, b in v.columns]

             .replace("rmse_har", "HAR error").replace("sans_sauts", "without jumps").replace("brute", "raw"))
tableau(v.reset_index().rename(columns={"horizon": "Horizon (sessions)"}))
Horizon (sessions) Average volatility (raw) Average volatility (without jumps) Persistence error (raw) Persistence error (without jumps) HAR error (raw) HAR error (without jumps)
5 0.297 0.286 0.205 0.181 0.156 0.139
20 0.318 0.305 0.116 0.101 0.102 0.089
60 0.323 0.309 0.093 0.086 0.092 0.084
120 0.323 0.310 0.106 0.094 0.101 0.092
  • Volatility: jumps inflate measured volatility by about 0.01 (1 point) and the forecast error by about 10%. But the ranking does not change: HAR beats persistence with or without jumps.
  • Price direction: the main model’s results are given in both readings, raw and control (Results page). No model beats the benchmark in either. The CC=F artefacts therefore do not explain the absence of signal.

Rainfall in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana

Why rainfall. Cocoa comes mainly from West Africa. Among the 9 countries tracked, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana together account for about half of production (FAOSTAT, weights used in the project). The cocoa tree needs regular rainfall:

  • a drought reduces flowering and bean size;
  • excess moisture favours diseases, such as black pod rot.

A poor rainy season can therefore reduce the harvest of the following months, and push the price up if the market had not anticipated it.

Show the code 
dernier = part.iloc[-1]
print(f"Weight in the production of the 9 countries tracked ({part.index[-1]}): Côte d'Ivoire {dernier['CIV']:.0%}, Ghana {dernier['GHA']:.0%}, "
      f"Indonesia {dernier['IDN']:.0%}, Ecuador {dernier['ECU']:.0%}.")
Weight in the production of the 9 countries tracked (2026): Côte d'Ivoire 41%, Ghana 11%, Indonesia 14%, Ecuador 9%.

How to read the chart. Each line compares rainfall over the last 3 months with the normal for the same months over 1991-2004. The gap is expressed in standard deviations, a measure of the usual gap from one year to the next.

  • 0: normal rainfall;
  • +1: clearly more rain than usual;
  • −1: clearly less;
  • beyond ±2: rare situation.
Show the code 
fig = go.Figure()
for i, (pays, nom) in enumerate([("CIV", "Côte d'Ivoire"), ("GHA", "Ghana")]):
    s = d[f"CHIRPS_ANOM3M_{pays}"]
    fig.add_scatter(x=s.index, y=s, mode="lines", name=nom, line=dict(width=2, color=SERIE[i]),
                    hovertemplate=f"{nom}<br>%{{x|%m/%Y}}: %{{y:.2f}} standard deviations<extra></extra>")
fig.add_hrect(y0=0, y1=6, fillcolor=SERIE[0], opacity=0.04, line_width=0)
fig.add_annotation(x=d.index[60], y=4.6, text="Wetter than normal", showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(color=ENCRE_2))
fig.add_annotation(x=d.index[60], y=-2.6, text="Drier than normal", showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(color=ENCRE_2))
fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color=MUET, width=1))
fig.update_layout(title="Rainfall over the last 3 months, deviation from normal (source: CHIRPS)", height=400,
                  yaxis=dict(title="Standard deviations", range=[-3, 5.2]))
fig.show()

What we observe.

  • The two countries often move together, since they are neighbours.
  • Early 2026 is far above normal, between +3 and +4.7 standard deviations. Note, however, that December to March is the dry season. Normal rainfall is low then, so a few showers are enough to produce a large deviation.
  • What the project concludes: these rainfall deviations did not improve the price forecast (Results page). Either the information is already absorbed by the market when it is published, or the effect on the harvest is too indirect to be captured.

Rainfall in millimetres and seasons

A standard deviation does not say how much it rained. The charts below give actual monthly rainfall in cocoa areas (CHIRPS, points weighted by the crop map), compared with its normal.

Show the code

The seasons are inferred from this climatology: main rainy season from March to June (peak in June, over 200 mm), short dry season in July-August, short rainy season in September-October, main dry season from November to February (less than 60 mm per month in December-February). Both countries share the same rhythm, Ghana slightly more contrasted.

Hover over a month to see observed rainfall, the normal, the deviation in standard deviations and the season. The models’ standard deviations use the 1991-2004 normal, prior to the sample, so that no future information enters it. The chart shows the 1991-2020 normal, the usual climatological reference, which is easier to read.

From climate to market: what lags?

The assumed chain is long. At each link, the table shows what the project was able to measure.

Step Assumed lag What the project measured
1. Climate conditions Observed to the day; published from 3 days (NASA) to 3-4 weeks (CHIRPS) Data collected, cross-checked between 3 sources
2. Crop development Several months between flowering and harvest (agronomic lag not quantified here) Not measured: no flowering or pod data
3. Yields Following season FAOSTAT yield unusable, estimated by FAO (Weather and production page)
4. Production October-to-September season No demonstrated effect of annual rainfall (p = 0.16)
5. World supply Known from market estimates, then from FAOSTAT at N+2 FAOSTAT production: information too late for the market
6. Market reaction As soon as the information is anticipated No improvement in out-of-sample forecasts

To look for a lag between rainfall and price, we measure the correlation between the 3-month rainfall deviation, at the time it is published, and the cocoa return over the 3 months starting 0 to 12 months later.

Show the code 
dl = lire("climat_delais.csv")
fig = go.Figure()
for k, (p, nom) in enumerate((("CIV", "Côte d'Ivoire"), ("GHA", "Ghana"))):
    x = dl[dl["pays"] == p]
    fig.add_scatter(x=x["delai_mois"] + (k - 0.5) * 0.18, y=x["rho"], mode="markers", name=nom, marker=dict(size=9, color=SERIE[k], line=dict(width=2, color="white")),
                    error_y=dict(type="data", symmetric=False, array=x["ic_haut"] - x["rho"], arrayminus=x["rho"] - x["ic_bas"], color=SERIE[k], thickness=2, width=3),
                    customdata=np.stack([x["delai_mois"], x["ic_bas"], x["ic_haut"]], axis=1),
                    hovertemplate=f"{nom}<br>Lag %{{customdata[0]}} months<br>Correlation %{{y:+.2f}}<br>95% CI: %{{customdata[1]:+.2f}} to %{{customdata[2]:+.2f}}<extra></extra>")
fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color=MUET, dash="dot"))
fig.update_layout(title="Published rainfall and cocoa return 3 months later, by lag (rank correlation)", height=380,
                  xaxis=dict(title="Lag between rainfall publication and the start of the return window (months)", dtick=1),
                  yaxis_title="Correlation")
fig.show()
  • Correlations are weak (−0.07 to +0.19) and almost all compatible with zero.
  • Only one out of 26 has an interval excluding zero: Ghana at 12 months (+0.17). With 26 trials, such an exception is expected by chance, and it does not survive a multiple-testing correction.
  • Correlations become slightly positive at 10-12 months: more rain would go with a price rise a year later, the opposite of the intuition “more rain, more supply”. This is a lead, not a result. One hypothesis would be excess moisture and diseases.
  • Conclusion: no climate lag emerges as usable for forecasting the price with these data. This is consistent with the model results.

El Niño

What it is. El Niño is a periodic warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean, recurring roughly every 2 to 7 years. It disrupts the weather in many regions. It is often associated with a more pronounced dry season in West Africa. La Niña is the opposite phenomenon: a cooling of the Pacific.

How to read the chart. NOAA’s ONI index measures the ocean temperature anomaly, in degrees.

  • Above +0.5 °C: El Niño episode.
  • Below −0.5 °C: La Niña episode.

According to our data, the strongest episodes since 2005 are those of 2015-2016, with a peak of +2.6 °C, and 2023-2024, with about +2.0 °C. A new strong episode appears in 2026.

Show the code 
s = d["ONI"]
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=s.index, y=s, mode="lines", line=dict(width=2, color=SERIE[0]), name="ONI",
                hovertemplate="%{x|%m/%Y}: %{y:+.2f} °C<extra></extra>")
fig.add_hrect(y0=0.5, y1=3, fillcolor=SERIE[1], opacity=0.08, line_width=0)
fig.add_hrect(y0=-3, y1=-0.5, fillcolor=SERIE[0], opacity=0.08, line_width=0)
fig.add_annotation(x=s.index[30], y=2.6, text="El Niño zone (above +0.5 °C)", showarrow=False, font=dict(color=ENCRE_2), xanchor="left")
fig.add_annotation(x=s.index[30], y=-2.6, text="La Niña zone (below −0.5 °C)", showarrow=False, font=dict(color=ENCRE_2), xanchor="left")
fig.update_layout(title="Oceanic Niño Index (ONI, NOAA), in °C", height=380, showlegend=False,
                  yaxis=dict(range=[-3, 3], title="°C"))
fig.show()

What the project concludes: as with rainfall, the El Niño index did not improve the price forecast. Episodes are announced months in advance by weather agencies: the market probably anticipates them.

Data quality control

Status definitions:

  • COMPLETE: all expected observations are present.
  • SURPLUS: more observations than expected.
  • INCOMPLETE: some observations are missing.
  • NOT APPLICABLE: source not queried or period not concerned.

A missing data point is not necessarily an error: days without a file in GDELT, series that start later, countries without a GPR index.

File inventory

The script scripts/34_inventaire_donnees.py checks that each expected file is present and complete.

Show the code 
DONNEES = {"Marches Yahoo": "Yahoo markets", "Prix Banque mondiale": "World Bank prices", "NASA POWER 7 variables": "NASA POWER 7 variables",
           "NASA rayonnement et vent": "NASA radiation and wind", "ERA5 pluie": "ERA5 rainfall", "ERA5 controle": "ERA5 control",
           "CHIRPS points": "CHIRPS points", "ENSO ONI": "ENSO ONI", "GEFS pluie": "GEFS rainfall", "GEFS temperature maximale": "GEFS maximum temperature",
           "Indices GEFS corriges": "Corrected GEFS indices", "Incendies FIRMS 2005-2025": "FIRMS fires 2005-2025", "Incendies FIRMS 2026": "FIRMS fires 2026",
           "Pesticides FAOSTAT": "FAOSTAT pesticides", "Azote FAOSTAT": "FAOSTAT nitrogen", "FAOSTAT cacao": "FAOSTAT cocoa",
           "ICCO editions (sensibilite)": "ICCO editions (sensitivity)", "CFTC historique": "CFTC legacy", "CFTC desagrege": "CFTC disaggregated",
           "Google Trends": "Google Trends", "GDELT presse cacao": "GDELT cocoa news", "GPR quotidien": "Daily GPR", "GPR mensuel": "Monthly GPR",
           "GDELT evenements": "GDELT events", "Base d'evenements": "Event database", "Points meteo": "Weather points", "Poids FAOSTAT": "FAOSTAT weights",
           "Dataset quotidien": "Daily dataset"}
inv = lire("inventaire_donnees.csv")
inv["famille"] = inv["famille"].map(FAMILIES | {"reference": "reference", "traite": "processed"}).fillna(inv["famille"])
inv["donnee"] = inv["donnee"].map(DONNEES).fillna(inv["donnee"])
inv["etat"] = inv["etat"].map({"complet": "complete", "incomplet": "incomplete"}).fillna(inv["etat"])
tableau(inv[["famille", "donnee", "attendu", "present", "etat"]].rename(columns={
    "famille": "Family", "donnee": "Data", "attendu": "Expected", "present": "Present", "etat": "Status"}))
